decks.title: Gravitation — Part 1: The universal law of gravitation
goals: State the universal law of gravitation and write its equation
Predict how the gravitational force changes when the masses or the separation change
Describe why the law is called universal and name its important effects

slides.heading: Why does the apple fall?
slides.body_md: Part 1 — the same pull that drops a ripe mango also keeps the Moon circling the Earth.

visual.alt: Flow from a mango on a tree to being pulled by the Earth to falling to the ground

slides.narration: A ripe mango drops from a branch and lands on the ground. Newton asked why it falls straight down and whether the same pull reaches as far as the Moon. His answer was one law for the whole universe.

slides.heading: Every body attracts every other body
slides.body_md: The force of attraction between any two bodies in the universe is called **gravitation**. It acts between a book and a desk, between two cricket balls and between the Sun and the planets. It is always an **attraction**, never a push.

rows: Yes, because the Earth is huge
Two cricket balls on a table
Yes, it keeps the Earth in its orbit

visual.alt: Table of three pairs of bodies and whether the gravitational attraction can be noticed

slides.narration: Gravitation acts between every pair of bodies, large or small. Two cricket balls on a table do attract each other, but the force is far too small to notice. When one body is as huge as the Earth, the pull becomes obvious.

slides.heading: The universal law of gravitation
slides.body_md: The force of attraction between two bodies is **directly proportional to the product of their masses** and **inversely proportional to the square of the distance between their centres**. It acts along the line joining the centres.

rows: Force increases in the same ratio
Force decreases much faster, as the square of the distance
Medium or position of other bodies
The pair of bodies is unaffected; the law holds everywhere

visual.alt: Table showing how the gravitational force depends on mass and on distance

slides.narration: Newton stated the law in two parts. The force grows with the product of the two masses. It falls with the square of the distance between their centres. Put both together and you get one equation with a constant called big gee.

slides.heading: What each symbol means
slides.body_md: In $F = \dfrac{G m_1 m_2}{r^2}$ the constant **G** is the same for every pair of bodies anywhere. It is called the **universal gravitational constant**.

rows: newton metre squared per kilogram squared

visual.alt: Table of the symbols in the law of gravitation with their meanings and SI units

slides.narration: F is the force in newtons. The two masses are in kilograms and the distance between their centres is in metres. The constant G has a very small value, which is why the force between everyday objects is too small to feel.

slides.heading: Quick check: the unit of G
slides.body_md: Work out the unit of G from the equation by making G the subject.

visual.alt: Table of the SI units of force, distance and mass

slides.narration: Rearrange the law to give G in terms of force, distance and mass. Which option is the correct unit of the gravitational constant?

slides.heading: A pair of equal and opposite forces
slides.body_md: Body 1 pulls body 2 with force $F$, and body 2 pulls body 1 with the **same** force $F$ in the **opposite** direction. The two forces act on **different bodies**, so they never cancel.

slides.narration: The pull is mutual. The first body attracts the second, and the second attracts the first with exactly the same strength, in the opposite direction. This is the third law of motion at work. Each arrow acts on a different body.

slides.heading: Quick check: the pull of a mango
slides.body_md: A mango is pulled towards the Earth. Think of the pair of forces.

visual.alt: Table of the two forces in the mango and Earth pair

slides.narration: The Earth pulls the mango downwards. What can you say about the pull of the mango on the Earth?

slides.heading: Changing the masses or the distance
slides.body_md: Work with **ratios**. If the masses are multiplied by $a$ and $b$ and the distance by $k$, the new force is $F \times \dfrac{ab}{k^{2}}$.

rows: one quarter of the old force
Both masses doubled and distance doubled

visual.alt: Table of how the gravitational force changes when the masses or the distance change

slides.narration: Do not recalculate from scratch. Double one mass and the force doubles. Double the distance and the force drops to a quarter. Halve the distance and it becomes four times larger. Double both masses and the distance together, and the force stays the same.

slides.heading: Worked example 1: a ratio problem
slides.body_md:
**Problem.** The force between two bodies is 12 N. The mass of the second body is doubled and the distance between them is tripled. Find the new force.

**Step 1.** The factor is $\dfrac{1 \times 2}{3^{2}} = \dfrac{2}{9}$.

**Step 2.** New force $= 12 \times \dfrac{2}{9} = 2.67$ N.

rows: two ninths of the old force

visual.alt: Table of the factors for each quantity in the ratio problem

slides.narration: Write the factor for each quantity. The masses give one and two. The distance is tripled, so divide by nine. The overall factor is two ninths. Multiply the old force by it, and the new force is about two point six seven newtons.

slides.heading: Quick check: two factors at once
slides.body_md: Use the ratio method for two changes together.

visual.alt: Table of the changes in one mass and in distance

slides.narration: The first mass is made three times larger and the distance is also made three times larger. By what factor does the force change?

slides.heading: The graph of force against distance
slides.body_md: For a fixed pair of bodies the force falls steeply as they move apart. Doubling the distance cuts the force to **a quarter**; quadrupling it cuts it to **one-sixteenth**.

visual.alt: Graph of gravitational force against distance, falling from sixty-four units at one unit of distance to sixteen at two and four at four
visual.caption: The inverse-square curve.

slides.narration: This curve shows a force dropping as the distance grows. From one unit to two units of distance, the force falls from sixty four to sixteen, which is one quarter. At four units it is only four. The curve never reaches zero but gets very small.

slides.heading: Worked example 2: the pull between two students
slides.body_md:
**Problem.** Two students of mass 55 kg and 65 kg sit 1.5 m apart. Find the gravitational force between them. ($G = 6.67 \times 10^{-11}$ N m² kg⁻²)

**Step 1.** $F = \dfrac{G m_1 m_2}{r^{2}} = \dfrac{6.67 \times 10^{-11} \times 55 \times 65}{1.5^{2}}$.

**Step 2.** $F = 1.06 \times 10^{-7}$ N.

rows: 1.06 × 10⁻⁷ N, about one ten-millionth of a newton

visual.alt: Table of the data and the answer for the force between two students

slides.narration: Put the numbers into the law. Multiply the constant by both masses and divide by the square of the distance. The answer is about one ten millionth of a newton, far too small to feel. That is why we do not drift towards each other.

slides.heading: Why the law matters
slides.body_md: The law explains many things at once. The same pull of the Earth makes bodies **fall**, makes the **Moon orbit** the Earth, holds the **planets** in orbit round the Sun and causes **tides**.

rows: Moon and the oceans, with help from the Sun

visual.alt: Table of four effects of gravitation and the bodies that attract

slides.narration: Newton showed that one law covers falling fruit and orbiting planets. The Earth holds the Moon, the Sun holds the planets, and the Moon lifts the ocean to make tides. Nothing in the sky needs a separate rule.

slides.heading: Summary: Part 1
bullets: Every body attracts every other body; the force acts along the line joining their centres.
The force is proportional to the product of the masses and inversely proportional to the square of the distance.
The equation is F = G m₁ m₂ / r², with G = 6.67 × 10⁻¹¹ N m² kg⁻².
The two forces of a pair are equal, opposite and act on different bodies.

visual.alt: Summary table of the changes in force

slides.narration: To sum up. Gravitation is a universal attraction. The force rises with the product of the masses and falls with the square of the distance. The forces on the two bodies are equal and opposite. Use ratios for quick answers.

slides.heading: Exam tips: Part 1
bullets: Measure the distance between the centres, not the surfaces.
For ratio questions, write the factor for each quantity before multiplying.
Write the unit of G when you substitute: N m² kg⁻².
Say that the two forces act on different bodies when asked why they do not cancel.

rows: Using the radius of a body as the distance
Use the distance between the centres
Saying the heavier body pulls harder on the lighter one

visual.alt: Table of three common slips and their fixes

slides.narration: Exam tips. Measure from centre to centre. Square the distance, and show the factor for each quantity in ratio problems. Remember that the two pulls of a pair are equal in size, whatever the masses may be.

decks.title: Gravitation — Part 2: Free fall, mass and weight
goals: Explain why all bodies fall with the same acceleration when air resistance is absent
Compare mass and weight in terms of definition, unit, nature and measuring instrument
Calculate the weight of a body from its mass in newton and kgf

slides.heading: Dropping things
slides.body_md: Part 2 — gravity pulls every falling body, heavy or light, with the same acceleration.

visual.alt: Flow from the gravity of the Earth to a body released to speed growing every second

slides.narration: Drop a stone from a bridge and watch it. It does not move at a steady speed. It speeds up all the way down. In this part we find how fast, and why a feather and a stone can fall together.

slides.heading: Gravity and the acceleration due to gravity
slides.body_md: The pull of the **Earth** on a body is called **gravity**. It gives every freely falling body the same acceleration, the **acceleration due to gravity**, $g$. Near the Earth, $g \approx 9.8$ m s⁻². Many problems use $g = 10$ m s⁻² and say so.

rows: Attraction by the Earth on a body
Acceleration of a body falling freely near the Earth, 9.8 m s⁻²

visual.alt: Table distinguishing gravitation, gravity and the acceleration due to gravity

slides.narration: Gravitation is the attraction between any two bodies. Gravity is the special case in which the Earth is one of the bodies. The acceleration it gives is about nine point eight metres per second every second. Many sums use ten for easy arithmetic.

slides.heading: Free fall
slides.body_md: A body is in **free fall** when gravity is the **only force** acting on it. In air, a feather falls slowly because **air resistance** is large for it. In a vacuum, a feather and a coin fall **together**.

rows: Air resistance affects the feather far more

visual.alt: Table comparing the fall of a feather and a coin in air and in a vacuum

slides.narration: In ordinary air the coin beats the feather, not because gravity favours the coin but because the air holds the feather back. Pump the air out of a long tube and both reach the bottom at the same moment.

slides.heading: Speed and distance in free fall
slides.body_md: Starting from rest, a falling ball gains speed $g t$ and covers a distance $\tfrac{1}{2} g t^{2}$ in time $t$ (with $g = 10$ m s⁻²). The gaps between pictures **grow** because the speed keeps increasing.

visual.alt: Strobe picture of a ball falling from rest, shown at one-second intervals with distances and speeds

slides.narration: In the strobe picture, the ball is photographed once every second. The gaps between positions get bigger and bigger. After one second it has fallen a little, after two seconds much more. Speed grows by the same amount each second.

slides.heading: Quick check: the strobe picture
slides.body_md: Read the distances in the strobe picture.

visual.alt: Table of the times and distances in the strobe picture

slides.narration: In the picture, the ball falls a short distance in the first second and a longer distance in each later second. What does this show?

slides.heading: Worked example 1: speed and distance after two seconds
slides.body_md:
**Problem.** A ball is dropped from rest. Find its speed and the distance fallen after 2 s. ($g = 10$ m s⁻²)

**Step 1.** $v = g t = 10 \times 2 = 20$ m s⁻¹.

**Step 2.** $s = \tfrac{1}{2} g t^{2} = \tfrac{1}{2} \times 10 \times 2^{2} = 20$ m.

visual.alt: Table of the working for the speed and distance after two seconds

slides.narration: Speed after two seconds is gee times time, ten times two, which is twenty metres per second. The distance is half of gee times time squared, half of ten times four, which is twenty metres.

slides.heading: Why heavy and light bodies fall together
slides.body_md: A body of mass $m$ feels a pull $mg$. The acceleration is force divided by mass: $a = \dfrac{mg}{m} = g$. The **mass cancels**, so every body has the same acceleration.

visual.alt: Table showing that a one kilogram and a four kilogram body both have acceleration g

slides.narration: A heavier body is pulled harder, but it also has more mass to move. The two effects cancel exactly. A one kilogram ball and a four kilogram ball have the same acceleration, so they reach the ground together.

slides.heading: Mass and weight
slides.body_md: **Mass** is the quantity of matter in a body. **Weight** is the force with which the Earth attracts the body: $W = m g$. Mass stays the same everywhere; weight depends on $g$ at the place.

rows: Force of gravity on the body
Vector, directed to the centre of the Earth

visual.alt: Table comparing mass and weight in meaning, unit, nature, instrument and variation with place

slides.narration: Mass tells how much matter there is, and it never changes. Weight is a force, and it depends on the place. Mass is measured in kilograms on a beam balance. Weight is measured in newtons on a spring balance.

slides.heading: Weight on a spring balance
slides.body_md: A spring balance shows weight. Its scale can be marked in **newton** or in **kilogram force (kgf)**. One kgf is the weight of a one-kilogram mass.

slides.heading: Quick check: reading the balance
slides.body_md: The pointer stands at 5 kgf, which is 49 N.

visual.alt: Table of the two readings of the spring balance

slides.narration: The body on the balance has a mass of five kilograms. Which statement about it is correct?

slides.heading: Newton and kilogram force
slides.body_md: $1\ \text{kgf} = 9.8$ N. To change kgf to newton, **multiply by 9.8**; to change newton to kgf, **divide by 9.8**. A body of mass $m$ kg weighs $m$ kgf.

visual.alt: Table of weights of three masses in kgf and in newton

slides.narration: The kilogram force is a larger unit than the newton. Multiply by nine point eight to go from kilogram force to newtons, and divide to come back. A mass of so many kilograms always weighs that many kilogram force.

slides.body_md:

sections.heading: 1. The universal law of gravitation
sections.body_md:
Every body in the universe attracts every other body. **Law:** the force of attraction between two bodies is directly proportional to the product of their masses and inversely proportional to the square of the distance between their centres. It acts along the line joining the centres.

$F = \dfrac{G\, m_1 m_2}{r^{2}}$, where $G = 6.67 \times 10^{-11}$ N m² kg⁻² has the same value everywhere (that is why it is called universal).

- The two forces of a pair are **equal and opposite** and act on **different bodies**, so they do not cancel. This follows the third law of motion.
- **Ratio method:** if the masses are multiplied by $a$ and $b$ and the distance by $k$, the force is multiplied by $\dfrac{ab}{k^{2}}$.
- **Importance:** the same law explains the fall of bodies, the orbit of the Moon round the Earth, the motion of planets round the Sun, the tides, and the motion of artificial satellites.
- The force between everyday objects is tiny because $G$ is tiny; it is noticeable only when at least one body is very massive.

The constant in the law of gravitation; 6.67 × 10⁻¹¹ N m² kg⁻² in SI units, the same for every pair of bodies.

sections.heading: 2. Gravity, acceleration due to gravity and free fall
sections.body_md:
**Gravity** is the force of attraction of the Earth on a body. A body released near the Earth speeds up; the acceleration it gains is the **acceleration due to gravity**, $g$, about 9.8 m s⁻² (10 m s⁻² where a question says so).

**Free fall:** motion under gravity alone, with no air resistance. Because the pull on a body of mass $m$ is $mg$, its acceleration is $\dfrac{mg}{m} = g$: the mass cancels, so **all bodies fall with the same acceleration**, whatever their masses.

- In air, a feather or a sheet of paper falls slower than a coin because of **air resistance**. In a vacuum tube both fall together.
- Starting from rest, after time $t$: speed $v = g t$ and distance $s = \tfrac{1}{2} g t^{2}$.
- The distances covered in successive equal intervals grow because the speed grows.

The motion of a body under the action of gravity alone.

sections.heading: 3. Mass and weight
sections.body_md:
**Mass** is the quantity of matter in a body; it is a scalar, measured in kilograms with a beam (physical) balance, and it is the same everywhere.

**Weight** is the force with which the Earth attracts a body: $W = m g$. It is a vector pointing towards the centre of the Earth, measured with a spring balance, and it changes with the place because $g$ changes. At a place where $g$ is smaller (for example on the Moon) the weight is smaller, but the mass is unchanged.

- SI unit of weight: **newton**. Gravitational unit: **kilogram force (kgf)**; $1\ \text{kgf} = 9.8$ N (about 10 N when $g = 10$ m s⁻² is used). A body of mass $m$ kg weighs $m$ kgf.
- Weight in newton $=$ weight in kgf $\times$ 9.8.

| Property | Mass | Weight |
|---|---|---|
| Meaning | Quantity of matter | Force of gravity on the body |
| SI unit | kilogram | newton |
| Nature | Scalar | Vector |
| Instrument | Beam balance | Spring balance |
| Varies with place | No | Yes |

Books differ on whether 1 kgf is taken as 9.8 N or 10 N; every problem here states the value used.

notes.exam_tips_md:
**Common mistakes**
- Measuring the distance from the surfaces instead of from the centres.
- Forgetting to square the distance in the law of gravitation.
- Writing the unit of weight as kg.
- Saying that a heavier body falls faster in a vacuum, or that mass changes from place to place.

**How marks are usually awarded**
- Statement of the law (2 marks): both proportionalities and the line of action.
- Numericals (1 to 3 marks): formula, substitution with units, answer with unit; for ratio problems, the factor for each quantity.
- Mass against weight (3 marks): definition, unit and instrument, one mark each.

questions.stem_md: The force of attraction between two bodies is F. State the new force when (i) the mass of one body is doubled, (ii) the distance between them is halved, (iii) both masses and the distance are doubled.

answer.model_answer_md:
**(i)** The factor is 2, so the force is **2F**.

**(ii)** The factor is $\dfrac{1}{(1/2)^2}$, so the force is **4F**.

**(iii)** The factor is $\dfrac{2 \times 2}{2^2} = 1$, so the force is **F** (unchanged).

questions.stem_md: A stone of mass 2 kg is released near the ground. (a) Find the force with which the Earth pulls it. (b) State the magnitude and direction of the force with which the stone pulls the Earth. (c) Why do we see only the stone move? (g = 10 m s⁻²)

answer.model_answer_md:
**(a)** $F = m g = 2 \times 10 = 20$ N.

**(b)** **20 N**, directed **upwards**, towards the stone.

**(c)** The same force gives the stone a large acceleration, but gives the Earth, whose mass is enormous, an **acceleration too small to notice**.

questions.solution_md: 20 N; 20 N upwards; huge mass of the Earth.

questions.stem_md: Two steel balls of mass 4 kg and 25 kg have their centres 0.5 m apart. Find the gravitational force between them, in units of 10⁻⁸ N. (G = 6.67 × 10⁻¹¹ N m² kg⁻²)
Two ships of mass 3 × 10⁶ kg and 5 × 10⁶ kg are 100 m apart. Find the gravitational force between them in newton. (G = 6.67 × 10⁻¹¹ N m² kg⁻²)
questions.solution_md: $F = \dfrac{G m_1 m_2}{r^2} = \dfrac{6.67 \times 10^{-11} \times 3 \times 10^{6} \times 5 \times 10^{6}}{100^2} = 0.1$ N.

questions.stem_md: The gravitational force between two bodies is 36 N. Find the force when the distance between them is tripled, the masses remaining the same.
questions.solution_md: $F_{\text{new}} = 36 \times \dfrac{1}{3^2} = 4$ N.

questions.stem_md: Two bodies attract each other with a force of 18 N. The mass of the first body is doubled, the mass of the second is tripled and the distance between them is doubled. Find the new force.
questions.solution_md: $F_{\text{new}} = 18 \times \dfrac{2 \times 3}{2^2} = 18 \times 1.5 = 27$ N.

options.text_md: the Earth pulls all bodies with the same force

questions.stem_md: A ball is dropped from the top of a tower 80 m high. Find (a) the time it takes to reach the ground and (b) its speed just before it lands. (g = 10 m s⁻²)

**(a)** $W = m g = 62 \times 9.8 = 607.6$ N.

**(b)** Weight in kgf = mass in kg = **62 kgf**.

questions.stem_md: A spring balance and a beam balance are each used to weigh the same body, first on the Earth and then at a place where g is smaller. Say which balance gives a different reading at the second place, and explain why the other does not.

answer.model_answer_md: The **spring balance** shows a **smaller** reading, because it measures the weight, which falls when g is smaller. questions.stem_md:
Two girls of mass 48 kg and 52 kg stand 2.0 m apart, the distance being measured between their centres. (G = 6.67 × 10⁻¹¹ N m² kg⁻²; g = 10 m s⁻²)

(a) Write the equation for the gravitational force between two bodies. [2]

(b) Calculate the force of attraction between the girls, in units of 10⁻⁸ N. [3]

(c) Find the force when they move to 1.0 m apart, using the ratio method. [2]

(d) The weight of the 48 kg girl is 480 N. Say about how many times this is larger than the pull in (b), and why the girls do not feel that pull. [3]

answer.model_answer_md:
**(a)** $F = \dfrac{G m_1 m_2}{r^2}$.

**(b)** $F = \dfrac{6.67 \times 10^{-11} \times 48 \times 52}{2^2} = 4.16 \times 10^{-8}$ N.

**(c)** The distance is halved, so the factor is $\dfrac{1}{(1/2)^2} = 4$ and $F = 4 \times 4.16 \times 10^{-8} = 16.6 \times 10^{-8}$ N.

**(d)** $\dfrac{480}{4.16 \times 10^{-8}}$ is about $1.2 \times 10^{10}$, so the weight is **about ten billion times larger**. The pull is far too small to notice beside the pull of the Earth and the friction at their feet, because G is tiny and their masses are small.

questions.solution_md: F = G m₁ m₂ / r²; 4.16 × 10⁻⁸ N; 16.6 × 10⁻⁸ N; about 10¹⁰ times, so the pull is negligible.

questions.stem_md:
A student drops a ball from a tower and records its distance fallen, s, at several times, t:

| t (s) | 0.5 | 1 | 1.5 | 2 |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| s (m) | 1.25 | 5 | 11.25 | 20 |

(a) Work out s ÷ t² for each reading and state what you notice. [3]

(b) Using s = ½ g t², find the value of g from your answer. [2]

(c) Find the speed of the ball at the end of 2 s. [2]

(d) State the shape of a graph of s against t², and say what its gradient represents. [3]

answer.model_answer_md:
**(a)** $s \div t^2$ is 5, 5, 5, 5, that is **5 m s⁻² every time**. The ratio is constant.

**(b)** $s = \tfrac{1}{2} g t^2$, so $\dfrac{s}{t^2} = \dfrac{g}{2}$ and $g = 2 \times 5 = 10$ m s⁻².

**(c)** $v = g t = 10 \times 2 = 20$ m s⁻¹.

**(d)** A **straight line through the origin**, because $s$ is proportional to $t^2$. Its gradient is $\tfrac{1}{2} g$, which is 5 m s⁻².

questions.solution_md: s/t² = 5 each time; g = 10 m s⁻²; 20 m s⁻¹; straight line through the origin with gradient g/2.

questions.stem_md:
A long glass tube contains a coin of mass 5 g and a small feather of mass 0.5 g. (g = 10 m s⁻²)

(a) The tube, full of air, is turned upside down quickly. State which object reaches the other end first and why. [2]

(b) The air is now pumped out and the tube is turned upside down again. State what is seen and what it shows. [2]

(c) Find the pull of the Earth on the coin and on the feather, and the ratio of the two pulls. Why are the two accelerations still equal? [3]

(d) The tube is 0.8 m long. In the vacuum, find the time the coin takes to fall through it and its speed on reaching the bottom. [3]

answer.model_answer_md:
**(a)** The **coin** reaches the bottom first, because the **air resistance** on the feather is large compared with its tiny weight.

**(b)** The coin and the feather reach the bottom **together**. This shows that, without air, **all bodies fall with the same acceleration**.

**(c)** Pull on the coin $= 0.005 \times 10 = 0.05$ N; on the feather $= 0.0005 \times 10 = 0.005$ N; ratio $= 10$. The coin has ten times the pull but also ten times the mass, so $a = \dfrac{mg}{m} = g$ for both.

**(d)** $s = \tfrac{1}{2} g t^2$: $0.8 = \tfrac{1}{2} \times 10 \times t^2$, $t^2 = 0.16$ and $t = 0.4$ s. Speed $v = g t = 10 \times 0.4 = 4$ m s⁻¹.

questions.solution_md: Coin first (air resistance); together in vacuum; 0.05 N, 0.005 N, ratio 10, same g; 0.4 s and 4 m s⁻¹.

marking_scheme.step: All bodies fall with the same acceleration

questions.stem_md:
A mango of mass 0.15 kg falls from a tree. (g = 10 m s⁻²; mass of the Earth = 6 × 10²⁴ kg)

(a) Find the force with which the Earth pulls the mango. [2]

(b) State the magnitude and direction of the force with which the mango pulls the Earth. [2]

(c) Find the acceleration that this force gives the Earth, and say how many times smaller it is than the acceleration of the mango. [3]

(d) Why is the motion of the Earth never noticed? [1]

(e) Explain why a mango of twice the mass would fall with the same acceleration. [2]

answer.model_answer_md:
**(a)** $F = m g = 0.15 \times 10 = 1.5$ N.

**(b)** **1.5 N**, directed **upwards**, towards the mango, as the forces of a pair are equal and opposite.

**(c)** $a = \dfrac{F}{M} = \dfrac{1.5}{6 \times 10^{24}} = 2.5 \times 10^{-25}$ m s⁻². The mango's acceleration is 10 m s⁻², which is about $4 \times 10^{25}$ times larger.

**(d)** The acceleration of the Earth is **absurdly small**, because its mass is enormous.

**(e)** The pull doubles but so does the mass, so the **mass cancels** in $a = \dfrac{mg}{m}$ and the acceleration stays equal to g.

questions.solution_md: 1.5 N; 1.5 N upwards; 2.5 × 10⁻²⁵ m s⁻², 4 × 10²⁵ times smaller; huge mass; mass cancels.
